São Paulo

Less than two months before the 2026 World Cup, Brazilians’ confidence in winning the title has reached its lowest level on record. According to a Datafolha survey, only 29% of the population believe the team led by Italian coach Carlo Ancelotti will win the tournament hosted by the United States, Canada and Mexico.

ORLANDO (USA), 31/03/2026 - CBF / BRAZIL vs CROACIA . (Foto: ANDRE DURAO/Agencia Enquadrar/Folhapress)

This figure is the lowest since tracking began in 1994. In addition, 46% of respondents expect Brazil will not advance beyond the quarterfinals, the stage at which the team was eliminated in 2018 and 2022. The pessimism reflects the loss of technical identity on the pitch and institutional crises at the Brazilian Football Confederation (CBF), which has had five presidents removed or arrested in the last seven terms.

Historically, confidence exceeded 56% until 2014, but the relationship was shaken after the 7–1 defeat to Germany. Currently, France appears as the main alternative to win the title, cited by 17% of respondents.

Datafolha surveyed 2,004 people aged 16 or older in 137 municipalities between April 7 and 9, 2026. The margin of error is two percentage points, plus or minus.

Spain are overwhelming favorites to win this Group H opener, and the underlying data supports that assessment. La Roja’s squad depth is unmatched at this tournament — their forward line alone (Yamal, Williams, Olmo, Oyarzabal) could trouble any defense in the world, and Rodri’s return to fitness gives them a control mechanism that makes even high-pressure opponents look disorganized.
[...]
Cabo Verde’s strengths — defensive organization, set pieces, and counter-attacking pace — are all areas where Spain’s experienced defensive structure (led by Pau Cubarsí, Marc Cucurella, and Alejandro Grimaldo) is well-equipped to cope. The Blue Sharks kept a flawless home record during CAF qualification, but those matches were played against teams from Africa’s second or third tier of footballing strength — a far cry from Spain’s technical and physical quality.
[...]
That said, Cabo Verde will not simply capitulate. Their emotional motivation at their first-ever World Cup will be immense, and if they can stay organized in the opening 20–25 minutes and keep the score level heading into the final third, they may find Spain growing impatient and vulnerable to a transition. The 4–2 loss to Chile in March showed a defensive fragility when faced with high-press, direct football — exactly what Spain will deploy.
[...]
